author: Katherine May
en_title: Wintering: Days That Seem to Lead Nowhere
zh_deck: 从九月的海滩到冬至，再到孩子暂时离校后的家庭安排。Katherine May写下的休整并不轻巧，也不是每种尝试都合用。
en_deck: A September beach, a winter solstice, and a child’s time away from school: May follows the work, missteps, and rearrangements within a season of interruption.

zh_title: 《过冬》：那些看起来没有进展的日子
zh_body:
Katherine May写的这个冬天，开始于九月的海滩。天气很好，她即将满四十岁，正在和朋友庆祝。丈夫却突然病倒，后来因阑尾炎住院。翻看那天留下的照片，晴朗的海边和接下来发生的事，简直不像属于同一天。

她原先的生活也已到了需要改变的时候。在丈夫发病之前，May已经决定离开大学的工作。后来，她自己的健康出现问题，儿子又因在学校承受的困扰而暂时离校。一件事还没有理顺，另一件便接着来了。一个人或许早知道人生不会始终顺利，轮到自己时，仍会觉得眼前这些日子像是走错了地方。

《过冬》从这份错位感写起。它是一部回忆录，也夹着旅行、自然观察和关于习俗的探访。章节沿着九月走到三月，时间仍在向前，生活却不按履历上那种方式前进。工作暂时放下了，家中需要重新安排，很多力气花在维持与等待上，难以说出究竟完成了什么。

书于2020年出版，后来被不少读者带进疫情中的生活。不过，它写的并非一次全球危机的共同经验，而是一个家庭先于别人进入的困顿。窗外的人照常出门，日程照常排满，自己却已经无法跟上。May用“过冬”为这样的处境取了一个名字，也沿着这个名字，走进了真正的寒冷。

## 她并没有把北方带回家

书中写到冰岛的地热浴池，也写芬兰人的桑拿。May对这些生活方式很向往，却没有写成一路照做、一路见效的体验报告。她尝试在英国延续桑拿的乐趣，身体却受不了，结果相当狼狈。

这次失败反而给书留下了可信的余地。一个人想向别处学习，不等于能把别人的日子完整移过来。读到一种办法时的心动，与身体实际接受它时的反应，可以完全不同。作者没有把不合用的部分剪掉，只给读者看一份成功的生活改造。

她在后来的访谈中解释，吸引自己的还不只是温度。按她的理解，桑拿在一些北方日常生活中提供了规律的间歇：与亲近的人相聚，从一天的事务中退开一会儿。对于外来的旅行者，那可能是特别的享受；对于长期过寒冬的人，它却嵌在日常安排之中。

因此，值得学的未必是一间热屋子。有一种生活给休整留好了位置，另一种生活却把所有空隙都当成尚未利用的时间，两者的区别远比项目名称更重要。只复制活动，却不改变使人疲惫的安排，效果自然有限。

书里关于北方的探访也没有一直停留在温暖舒适的画面。准备冬季，需要劳动，需要预先照料生活的条件。寒冷并不会因为人欣赏它的美就变得好过。在这里，“接受冬天”有很实际的一面：知道它会来，便不能继续按夏天的办法安排一切。

对已经筋疲力尽的May来说，这个差别很要紧。她原先习惯把身体的变化看成干扰，盼着干扰消失，好回到既定计划。如今，她试着反过来，让计划回应已经发生的变化。书的行文也跟着慢了下来；旅行不再只负责抵达目的地，一个不适合自己的尝试，同样值得记下。

## 冬至不是一项个人成绩

May还到巨石阵度过冬至。这样一个场合，很容易被写成充满启示的神秘时刻；她却对仪式既受吸引，又有些不好意思。她并非早已确信某套信仰，只是想知道，人们怎样一起承认一个季节的转折。

在与Krista Tippett的访谈中，她谈到德鲁伊传统的实践者Philip Carr-Gomm，也谈到他的幽默。他并不避讳这些仪式在外人眼中有点古怪。这使May感到亲近：她可以认真对待某种需要，同时不必假装自己的怀疑已经全部消失。

这种不完全确信，给《过冬》带来了与励志书不同的语气。作者不是找到了一种答案，再回头教读者照办。她仍在尝试，仍会尴尬，也未必知道某种仪式将来是否会成为自己生活的一部分。

冬至的作用，在于它不由个人表现决定。事情做得好不好，这一天都会到来。对于一段无法预测何时结束的困难，这样的时间标记可以暂时把人从自己的进度表中带出来：除了工作是否完成、身体是否好转，世界还有别的变化可看，也有人一起看。

但书中的季节线索并没有因此成为病程表。日照会渐长，不代表人的困境也一定按时减轻。May的比喻最动人之处，是给孤立的经验找到一种可讲述的形状；它若被当成恢复的保证，反而会失去分寸。春天没有解决的问题，仍然需要具体去解决。

## 儿子停课以后，谁的时间要改变

书里的另一条线索，比旅行更难安排。May的儿子在学校过得很艰难，她最终让他暂时离校。她没有把自己写成一位早已向往在家教育的母亲。恰恰相反，她原本需要自己的时间，也从未打算这样生活。

这一点使她的选择有了重量。接受一个孩子的困难，意味着自己的日程也得受影响。孩子不去学校，白天便不能继续照旧；家中的钱和精力都要重新盘算。这里没有从容选择另一种教育方式的漂亮全景，只有一家人发现原来的办法已经行不通，先停下来，再想下一步。

May后来告诉Tippett，孩子回到了另一所学校，适应得很好。她回看那段时间，最看重的是孩子发现：把难受告诉父母，能够引起实际的回应。听见这句话，我们才更清楚地知道，暂停究竟做了什么。它不只是减少压力，也改变了孩子对求助的认识。

把这一段与前面的北方旅行放在一起，《过冬》的重心便从个人感受移到了共同生活。给自己一点余地，可以从取消某个安排开始；给孩子一点余地，却可能要拿出自己并不富余的时间。两者都叫休整，承担的工作并不一样。

这也是书中值得保留的一处不轻松。照顾别人和保存自己，不会因为原则上都重要，就自然达到平衡。May能讲述这次调整，是因为家人确实作了安排，也承受了后果。对于另一户家庭，办法可能不同，还需要学校或其他支持。读她的经历，能学到的首先是认真辨认问题，而不是直接搬用她的决定。

## 这本书没有替我们过冬

《过冬》受到欢迎，与它给停顿提供了较温和的说法有关。有些读者却指出，作者能够离职、旅行、调整家庭生活，这些条件不是人人都有。这个批评不能靠“每个人都能抽出一点时间”轻轻回答。对有些人来说，缺少的恰恰不是休息意愿，而是少挣一份收入以后，账单由谁来付。

不过，May写作中也有一些东西，抵抗着把本书变成舒适生活的消费指南。桑拿不合身体，照顾孩子打乱计划，仪式伴着尴尬；这些不顺利没有被删去。她写的更像摸索中的生活，而不是一组可供照搬的风格。

问题也因此应当问得更准确。旅行有没有给她帮助，与旅行是不是所有人都负担得起，是两个问题。我们可以相信前者，又不把它推荐成普遍处方。同样，承认停止工作有时必要，也不该掩盖一个人可能根本没有这样的条件。回忆录使人理解一种经验，不能代替让更多人获得照顾的实际安排。

这本书的散漫也有代价。它从家庭转到传说，又走进自然，期待系统论证的读者可能觉得线索不够集中。但这样的往返，使困难的日子不只剩下“我出了什么问题”这一件事。May还会看天气，会对别处的生活好奇，会有一次不怎么成功的尝试。生病和停顿并没有耗尽她对世界的兴趣。

或许这正是《过冬》值得慢慢读的原因。它把一个看起来缺乏进展的季节写得有了细部，也让我们看见，调整生活远没有一句“慢下来”那么轻巧。从九月翻到三月，变化不只在窗外。有些事被放下，有些关系换了相处的办法，还有些问题没有答案。它们共同构成了这段日子，而不必等生活恢复正常以后，才算真正发生过。
en_body:
Katherine May’s winter begins on a beach in September. The weather is fine, she is approaching forty, and she is celebrating with friends. Then her husband becomes seriously ill and is hospitalized with appendicitis. Looking back at photographs, the sunny seaside and what followed seem scarcely to belong to the same day.

Her life had already reached a point of change. Before her husband became ill, she had decided to leave her university job. Later her own health deteriorated, and difficulties at school led her son to withdraw temporarily. Before one problem was settled, another arrived. Knowing in principle that life cannot always run smoothly offers little preparation for the feeling that these particular days have somehow gone wrong.

Wintering begins with that dislocation. It is a memoir interwoven with travel, observations of nature, and investigations of customs. Its chapters move from September to March. Time advances, but life does not progress as it does on a résumé. Work is set aside, the household rearranged, and considerable effort spent on maintenance and waiting, with little that can be described as an accomplishment.

Published in 2020, the book accompanied many readers through the pandemic. Its subject, however, is not a shared global emergency but a household entering difficulty before those around it. Outside, people go to work and fill their calendars as usual. Inside, keeping pace has become impossible. “Wintering” gives May a name for this condition and leads her toward actual cold.

## She did not bring the North home intact

May writes about geothermal pools in Iceland and Finnish saunas. These ways of living attract her, but the book is not a succession of experiments that work beautifully. When she tries to continue enjoying saunas in Britain, her body does not cooperate. The experience goes badly.

That failure adds credibility. Wanting to learn from another place does not mean being able to transplant its life. Being attracted to a practice while reading about it and discovering what one’s body makes of it are different experiences. May does not edit out what failed to fit, leaving only a successful lifestyle transformation.

In a later interview she explained that temperature was not the whole attraction. As she understood it, sauna in some northern communities provides a regular pause in daily life: time with people close to you and a temporary withdrawal from demands. For a visitor this might be a special indulgence. For those accustomed to long winters, it can be part of an ordinary arrangement.

What deserves attention, then, is not necessarily a heated room. One way of life makes room for recovery, while another treats every interval as unused time. That difference matters more than the name of the activity. Copying the activity without changing exhausting arrangements has obvious limits.

Her northern explorations do not remain entirely within scenes of comfort. Preparing for winter involves work and advance care for the conditions of living. Appreciating cold weather does not make it easy to endure. Accepting winter has a practical side: knowing it will arrive means recognizing that summer arrangements cannot simply continue.

This matters to an already exhausted May. She had tended to experience changes in her body as interruptions and hope they would disappear so that the plan could resume. Now she tries to let the plan answer to what has changed. The writing slows accordingly. A journey need not justify itself solely by arrival; an unsuccessful attempt also deserves space.

## The solstice is not a personal achievement

May also visits Stonehenge for the winter solstice. Such an occasion could easily become a scene of unquestioned revelation. Instead she is attracted to ritual and slightly embarrassed by it. She has not already committed herself to a settled faith. She wants to understand how people mark a seasonal turning together.

Talking with Krista Tippett, she discussed the Druid practitioner Philip Carr-Gomm and his humor. He did not deny that these rituals could look odd from outside. May found that companionable. She could take a need seriously without pretending all her doubts had gone away.

The incomplete conviction gives Wintering a different voice from a motivational manual. This is not an author who has found the answer and returned to instruct the rest of us. She is still trying things, still awkward, and unsure whether a ritual will eventually become part of her own life.

The solstice matters partly because it does not depend on performance. It arrives whether work is going well or badly. During a difficulty with no predictable end, such a marker can briefly release someone from a private progress chart. Besides whether a task is finished or a body recovering, the world has other changes to notice, and other people can notice them together.

But the book’s seasonal pattern is not a medical timetable. Lengthening daylight does not ensure that personal difficulty will diminish on schedule. May’s metaphor is most moving when it gives an isolated experience a shape that can be communicated. Turn it into a promise of recovery and it loses its proportion. Problems that remain in spring still need concrete responses.

## When a child leaves school, whose time changes?

Another strand is harder to organize than travel. May’s son is having a very difficult time at school, and she eventually withdraws him temporarily. She does not present herself as a mother who has always dreamed of educating at home. On the contrary, she needs time of her own and had never intended to live this way.

That makes the decision substantial. Acknowledging the child’s distress means accepting consequences for her own schedule. Without school, the daytime cannot continue as before. Money and energy have to be reconsidered. This is not a polished panorama of calmly selecting an alternative education. A family discovers that the existing arrangement no longer works, pauses it, and looks for the next step.

May later told Tippett that her son had returned to a different school and was doing well. Looking back, she especially valued his discovery that telling his parents about distress could produce an actual response. This clarifies what the pause accomplished. It did more than reduce pressure; it changed what asking for help meant.

Placed beside the northern journeys, this moves the book from private feeling toward shared life. Making room for oneself might begin by canceling a commitment. Making room for a child can require time one does not have to spare. Both might be called recovery, but they involve different work.

The unresolved difficulty is worth retaining. Caring for others and preserving oneself do not automatically balance simply because both matter. May can describe this adjustment because a family made arrangements and bore consequences. Another household might need a different solution or more support from school and elsewhere. The first thing to learn is to identify the problem seriously, not reproduce her decision.

## The book cannot winter on our behalf

Part of Wintering’s appeal lies in its gentler language for interruption. Some readers object that leaving work, traveling, and rearranging family life require resources not everyone possesses. “Anyone can take a little time” does not answer this. For some people the missing thing is not willingness to rest but someone to pay the bills when earnings stop.

Yet aspects of May’s writing resist turning the book into a catalogue of comfortable living. The sauna disagrees with her, childcare disrupts plans, ritual brings embarrassment. These failures remain. She offers life being worked out, rather than a style ready for imitation.

This allows a more accurate question. Whether travel helped her and whether everyone can afford it are different matters. We can accept the former without making it a universal prescription. Likewise, recognizing that a pause from work may be necessary must not obscure the fact that someone may lack that option. A memoir helps us understand an experience; it cannot replace arrangements that give more people care.

The book’s wandering has a cost too. It moves from family to traditional stories to nature, and readers wanting systematic argument may find the threads loose. But these excursions keep difficulty from shrinking to the single question of what is wrong with the narrator. May still watches the weather, wonders about other lives, and attempts something that does not work. Illness and interruption have not exhausted her curiosity.

That may be the best reason to read slowly. A season that appears unproductive acquires detail, and adjusting a life proves far less simple than telling someone to slow down. From September to March, the changes are not only outdoors. Some things are relinquished, some relationships rearranged, and some questions remain unanswered. Together they make these days a part of life, without waiting for normality to return before they count.
